rv.q: It’s definitely worth the trip to West 42nd Street to find this little corner of untouched Texas.
Time hasn't been kind to Lone Star , which depicts toxic hypermasculinity, unbridled bigotry, and veiled homophobia with a sort of commonplace shrug.
Fortunately, the fun of McLure’s Lone Star still holds up, as does the portrayal of a damaged war veteran.

Lone Star loses its way as it propels forward, with slow brother Ray not really as out of touch as he seems, macho Roy dealing with the trauma of PTSD, long-suffering Elizabeth, and the nerd Cletis, who’s managing his father’s appliance store and is better off than the brothers.

cn.t: This 1970s Texas dramedy about a PTSD-afflicted Vietnam vet receives mixed reviews, with critics questioning whether McLure's dated one-act merits revival despite committed performances that mine more pathos than comedy.
